out.story: Valid and invalid ad clicks arrive on Kafka (the clicks topic published by {{ad-click-tracking-and-fraud|click tracking}}). `ClickAggregator` runs in the worker app (`AdsWorkerModule`). It reads each batch and counts clicks per campaign and per minute. It writes the counts to the `ads.click-aggregates` topic. The counts and the consumer offsets of that batch go out in one Kafka transaction, so a crash means nothing is visible and the batch is read again. Every hour at minute 5, the `ads.bill-hour` job bills the previous hour. It sums the minute counts per campaign from the ClickHouse `ad_click_minute` table. For each campaign, `charge` runs in one database transaction. It locks the campaign row and works out how much the campaign already spent that day. The charge is clicks times cost per click, capped by what is left of the daily budget. It inserts an `AdBillingRun` row, which is the once-per-(campaign, hour) guard, and then posts an `AD_CHARGE` journal through the ledger: the shop account pays, and the platform fees account receives. Every day at 02:30, `ads.reconcile-day` recounts yesterday from the raw, deduplicated `ad_clicks_raw` table in ClickHouse. If an hour was never billed, it charges it. If the billed click count differs from the exact one, `adjust` posts an `ADJUSTMENT` journal for the difference (a refund if the shop was over-billed) and marks the run as reconciled. The batch path is the source of truth.
out.summary: Ad clicks from Kafka are counted per minute with exactly-once transactions, then billed to shops hourly through the ledger and corrected daily from the raw click log.

out.story: When `GET /ads/sponsored` serves an ad, `AdsService.sponsored` makes a click token for it. The token holds the impression id, campaign, shop, product and an expiry 30 minutes ahead. It is signed with an HMAC (a keyed hash). The ad's `clickUrl` points at `/api/ads/click/<token>`. Because the token is signed, nobody can forge a campaign id. Because it is tied to an impression, each impression can be billed only once. See {{click-token}}. When the user clicks, `AdsController.click` hands the token and the client IP to `AdsService.click`. The IP comes from the `cf-connecting-ip` header, or from `req.ip` if that header is missing. The service checks the signature and expiry. It then runs the fraud checks in order: {{impression-dedupe}}, then {{ip-burst-filter}}. It publishes the result to Kafka ({{click-publishing}}) and, if the click is valid, adds the campaign's cost per click to the day's spend counter in Redis. The user is always redirected with a 302 to the front-end product page, even if the token is bad, expired, duplicated or flagged as fraud. A bad token goes to `/`. A fraud-filtered click still lands on the product but is not billed. The response is `no-store` so every click reaches the server. Later billing is covered in {{ad-click-aggregation-and-billing}}, and serving in {{sponsored-ad-campaigns}}.
out.summary: `GET /ads/click/:token` checks a signed ad click token, filters fraud with Redis, always redirects the user to the product, and publishes the click to Kafka.

out.story: `adjust` is a private method in `AdBillingJobs`. The daily job {{daily-reconciliation|`reconcileDay`}} calls it when a billed hour has not been reconciled yet and its billed click count differs from the exact count in the raw click log. It gets the campaign, the hour, the clicks that were billed and the exact clicks. Everything runs in one database transaction. First it reads the shop and the price per click from `AdCampaign`. It then works out the money difference: `(exactClicks - billedClicks) * cpcCents`. A positive number means the shop was under-billed. A negative number means the shop gets a refund. See {{adjustment-amount}}. Next it updates the `AdBillingRun` row for that campaign and hour. It sets the reconciled click count and stores the new journal id, but only if the reconciled click count is still empty. This is the once-only guard, see {{reconcile-once-guard}}. If no row was updated, or the difference is 0, it stops. Otherwise it posts an `ADJUSTMENT` journal through the ledger and logs the change. See {{adjustment-journal}}.
out.summary: `adjust` fixes one already-billed campaign hour by marking its billing run as reconciled and posting an `ADJUSTMENT` ledger journal worth the click difference times the price per click.

parts.title: Signed money difference in cents
parts.what: The value `delta`, calculated as exact clicks minus billed clicks, times the price per click in cents.

parts.title: Journal lines that follow from the sign
parts.what: The shop account gets `-delta` and `PLATFORM_FEES` gets `+delta`, so the journal sums to zero.

out.story: When the daily reconciliation finds a billed hour whose click count differs from the exact count in the raw click log, it calls `adjust`. See {{daily-reconciliation}} and {{adjust-journal}}. `adjust` first loads the campaign's shop and its price per click in cents (`cpcCents`). It then works out the signed difference: `(exactClicks - billedClicks) * cpcCents`. A positive number means the shop was under-billed and owes more. A negative number means it was over-billed and gets a refund. Zero means no money moves. The sign then drives the ledger journal. The shop account gets `-delta` and the platform fees account gets `+delta`. So a positive difference takes money from the shop, and a negative one gives it back. The difference is not capped by the daily budget, unlike a normal charge in {{hourly-billing}}.
out.summary: `adjust` computes a signed cent amount, (exact clicks minus billed clicks) times the campaign's price per click, and uses it to under-bill or refund one campaign hour.

gotchas: The filter can say "might exist" for a code that does not exist. Those codes still go on to the cache and DynamoDB and end up as `null`.
If Redis is down, the filter lets every code through. During an outage, scans of made-up codes reach DynamoDB.
The filter is only filled by `create`. A link that is in DynamoDB but was never added to the filter would be rejected as unknown.

parts.title: Filter size of 100 million codes at 1% false positives
parts.what: The constructor creates `RedisBloomFilter` with the key `share-links:bloom`, a capacity of 100,000,000 and an error rate of 0.01.

parts.title: Adding each new code to the filter when a link is created
parts.what: After the DynamoDB write succeeds, `create` calls `bloom.add` with the new code, so real codes are never rejected.

parts.title: Checking the filter before any lookup in resolve
parts.what: `mightContain` returns false for a code that never existed, and `resolve` then returns `null` without touching the cache or DynamoDB.

parts.title: Letting everything through when Redis errors
parts.what: A `.catch(() => true)` on `mightContain` means a Redis failure acts like "might exist", so the lookup carries on to the cache and DynamoDB.

out.story: Short links are looked up by code on every redirect, and people can scan random codes to find links. The Bloom filter is a cheap first guard. It is a compact structure that can say "this code was definitely never created" or "it might exist". It never forgets a real code, but it sometimes says "might exist" for a fake one. The filter is the `RedisBloomFilter` class, kept in Redis under the key `share-links:bloom`. `ShareLinkService` builds it in its constructor, sized for 100 million codes at a 1% false-positive rate. When `create` stores a new link in DynamoDB, it then calls `bloom.add([code])` to record the code in the filter. When {{resolve-pipeline|resolve}} runs, it checks the code format first. Then it calls `mightContain(code)`. If the answer is no, `resolve` returns `null` at once, with no cache or DynamoDB call. If the answer is yes, the lookup goes on to the cache and DynamoDB. If Redis fails, the `.catch(() => true)` in `resolve` treats the code as "might exist", so real links still work.
out.summary: A Redis-backed Bloom filter that quickly says whether a short code could ever have been created, so lookups for made-up codes stop before the cache or DynamoDB.

data.name: Links (DynamoDB)

gotchas: A missing code is cached for only 60 seconds, so a freshly created link or alias can look missing for up to a minute unless `create` clears the key, which it does.
Stale data can be served for up to 24 hours while a refresh runs, so edits to a link may not show up instantly.
Expiry is checked after the cache returns, so a link with `expiresAtEpoch` in the past can sit in the cache but still resolves to `null`.
Changing the key layout means changing `v1` in `linkCacheKey`, since old entries are otherwise read as-is.

parts.what: `linkCacheKey` turns a code into `link:v1:<code>`, and `create` uses the same key to clear stale entries.

parts.title: Fresh time, stale time and not-found time
parts.what: The options passed to `getOrLoad` are 1 hour fresh (`ttlMs`), 24 hours stale-while-revalidate (`swrMs`), 60 seconds for a cached miss (`negativeTtlMs`), and a `hot` in-process layer (`l1`).

parts.title: Loader that reads one link from DynamoDB
parts.what: A function that does a `GetCommand` by `code` on the `Links` table and returns the item or `null`.

out.story: `resolve` in `ShareLinkService` calls `getOrLoad` on the shared `CacheService` after the format check and the Bloom filter have let a code through (see {{resolve-pipeline}}). You pass it a cache key, a loader function, and a few timing options. The key comes from `linkCacheKey`, which builds `link:v1:<code>`. The `v1` is a version tag, so the key layout can change later without reading old entries. On a cache hit, you get the stored link right away. On a miss, `getOrLoad` runs the loader. The loader does a DynamoDB `GetCommand` on the `Links` table and returns the item, or `null` if there is none. The result goes into the cache for 1 hour. After that hour, the old copy can still be served for up to 24 hours while a refresh happens (stale-while-revalidate), so a slow DynamoDB does not slow down the redirect. A `null` result is cached too, but only for 60 seconds. That is the negative cache. Repeated lookups for a code that does not exist skip DynamoDB. The short timer means a mistake fixes itself quickly. When `create` claims a code, it calls `cache.invalidate` on the same key. That drops any cached "not found" for a just-claimed alias. Back in `resolve`, an expired link is still dropped after the cache returns it, because expiry is checked on the returned value.
out.summary: `getOrLoad` is a cache lookup that stores a link for an hour, serves old copies while it refreshes, and briefly remembers that a code was not found.

out.story: `LinkClicked` is defined at the top of `share-link.service.ts` with `defineEvent('link.clicked', 'links', 1, ...)`. That helper gives the event a name, a topic (`links`) and a version number (1). The payload shape is a `zod` object, so the data is checked against it. Three fields are required strings: a unique click id, the link code and a timestamp. Three more are optional: country, referer and a flag for whether the edge already saw the click. If they are missing, `zod` fills in an empty string, an empty string and `false`. The event is built in `recordClick`. It makes a fresh click id with `uuidv7()`, stamps the time as an ISO string, cuts the referer to 300 characters, and turns missing country or edge values into the defaults. It then sends the event to Kafka without waiting. See {{fire-and-forget-click-recording}} for that part, and {{link-click-analytics}} for what consumes the event.
out.summary: `LinkClicked` is a typed, versioned `link.clicked` event that describes one click on a share link, with three required strings and three optional details that fall back to empty or false.

parts.title: Validating a signed token (verifyClick)

out.story: When an ad is served, a click token is generated that signs a payload containing the impression id, campaign id, shop id, price, and a 30-minute expiry. The token is a compact string: `payload.mac` where the payload is the base64url-encoded claims and the mac is a truncated HMAC-SHA256 signature. When a user clicks and sends the token to the backend in {{ad-click-tracking-and-fraud}}, the server calls `verifyClick` to recompute the signature in constant time, decode the claims, and reject the token if it's expired. This stateless check proves the impression was real and hasn't been forged.
out.summary: A base64url JSON payload plus a truncated HMAC-SHA256 signature, verified in constant time and rejected once expired.

out.story: After `reconcileDay` gets the exact valid-click count per campaign and hour from the raw click log ({{exact-click-query}}), it looks at each one in turn. It reads the matching `AdBillingRun` row (the table that holds one billing record per campaign and hour). That row has `clicks`, the count that was billed, and `reconciledClicks`, which stays empty until the hour has been corrected. There are three outcomes. If there is no row, the hourly job never billed that hour, so `charge` bills it with the exact count. If a row exists, `reconciledClicks` is still empty and the billed `clicks` differs from the exact count, `adjust` fixes it ({{adjust-journal}}). In every other case nothing happens. It reads the campaign row and locks it with `FOR UPDATE`, so two charges for the same campaign can't run at the same time. In the same query it adds up what `AdBillingRun` already holds for that campaign on that calendar day. That sum is the money already spent today. If the campaign does not exist, it returns 0. out.story: Clicks flow from {{ad-click-tracking-and-fraud}} into Kafka's `ads.clicks` topic, where `ClickAggregator` reads them in batches. The service groups each batch's clicks by campaign and minute (counting valid vs invalid clicks), then atomically writes the aggregates to `ads.click-aggregates` and commits the consumer group's offset in a single Kafka transaction. If anything fails during the transaction—parsing, sending aggregates, sending offsets—the entire transaction aborts. No aggregates become visible to read_committed readers. The batch is re-delivered from the last committed offset, and the aggregator processes it again. Because each aggregate is keyed by campaign, minute, partition, and first offset of the batch, re-delivering a batch safely overwrites the prior aggregates instead of duplicating them. The exactly-once guarantee holds: each click is counted exactly once across failures and restarts.
out.summary: Aggregates clicks per minute and commits them with consumer offsets in a single Kafka transaction, re-delivering the batch on failure.

out.story: When people create short affiliate links, you want the resulting codes to look random so visitors can't guess other people's links or predict codes in order. Instead of generating and checking random codes until you find one that's free, `scramble` uses a Feistel network—a mathematical permutation that maps every sequential ID (1, 2, 3, …) to a unique "random-looking" number, then encodes it as a 7-character base62 string. The `scramble` function does 4 rounds of HMAC-SHA256 mixing using a secret key. Because a Feistel network is a permutation by design, every ID maps to exactly one code and every code maps back to exactly one ID (via `unscramble`), with no collisions and no uniqueness checks needed. The key ensures different services or instances produce different scrambles from the same IDs. With 40 bits of ID space, you get 1.1 trillion unique codes. When a user creates a link, you lease a sequential ID from {{id-lease}}, scramble it with your key to get a number, convert that to base62 via `toBase62` to get the 7-character code, and store it alongside the link destination in {{share-short-links}}.
out.summary: Scramble turns sequential IDs into random-looking 7-character codes using a keyed Feistel cipher, preventing link enumeration.

gotchas: IDs must fit in exactly 40 bits (0 to 1,099,511,627,775); passing an ID outside this range throws a RangeError immediately.
The `key` parameter completely determines the output: the same ID with different keys produces completely different codes, so the key must be consistent and kept secret like any cryptographic key.
A Feistel network is always a bijection, so every ID maps to exactly one unique code—no collisions occur, which is why there's no collision checking or retry loop in the code.
You cannot reverse a scrambled code to its ID without the key and the original algorithm; to an attacker with only the code it's one-way, but with the key it's perfectly reversible.

parts.title: 40-bit ID space and 4-round Feistel network configuration
parts.what: `HALF_BITS = 20` splits the ID into two 20-bit halves (1.1 trillion possible codes, fitting in 62^7); `ROUNDS = 4` provides the rounds for cryptographic strength.

parts.title: Decrypt a scrambled number back to the original ID
parts.what: `unscramble(value, key)` runs the 4 Feistel rounds in reverse order (from round 3 down to 0) with the same key to undo the encryption and recover the original ID.

parts.title: One round of HMAC-SHA256-based mixing
parts.what: `round(key, r, half)` computes HMAC-SHA256 of the key and the string "r:half", masks the result to 20 bits, and returns it to be XORed with the other half.

out.story: When sequential IDs are exposed (link IDs 1, 2, 3, ...), attackers can enumerate all links by guessing. This cipher prevents that by encrypting IDs into random-looking codes using a Feistel network. The 40-bit ID is split into two 20-bit halves; for 4 rounds, each round applies `round` (HMAC-SHA256 of the round number and the right half) and XORs it with the left half, then swaps the halves. A Feistel network is a mathematical bijection—every ID maps to exactly one unique code—so no collisions occur and no collision checking is needed. The scrambled number is encoded as 7 base-62 characters (0-9A-Za-z) via `toBase62`, creating a short random-looking code. To reverse it, `unscramble` runs the rounds in reverse order, undoing the encryption to recover the original ID. This reversibility is essential: when you need to recover the ID from a code (like looking up link details), the same key and algorithm decrypt it perfectly.
out.summary: A 4-round Feistel network using HMAC-SHA256 creates a one-to-one mapping from sequential 40-bit IDs to random-looking numbers and back.

Then it decides whether to record the click. The edge worker can serve cached redirects itself and tells the origin it already counted the click by sending the header `x-edge-click-recorded: 1`. If that header is anything else, the controller calls `recordClick` with the country (from `cf-ipcountry`) and the referer. `recordClick` is a plain method, not an async one. It builds a {{link-clicked-event|`link.clicked` event}} with a fresh time-ordered `uuidv7` click id, the code, the current time, the country, the referer cut to 300 characters, and the via-edge flag. It hands the event to the Kafka producer, with the code as the message key. It does not await the send. The controller then sets the `ref` query parameter to the code, adds `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=10`, and answers with a 302. out.story: `billHour` is the handler for the `ads.bill-hour` job. It runs at minute 5 of every hour, with one run at a time. It works on the previous full hour unless a job payload gives a specific hour. It asks ClickHouse for the sum of clicks per campaign from the `ad_click_minute` table for that hour, skips campaigns with zero clicks, and then calls `charge` for each campaign. It returns how many campaigns it saw and the total cents charged. The minute sums come from {{ad-click-aggregation-and-billing|the click aggregation pipeline}}. `charge` does the real work inside one Postgres transaction. It locks the campaign's `AdCampaign` row with `FOR UPDATE`, so two charges for the same campaign can't run side by side. In the same query it adds up what the campaign has already been billed today from `AdBillingRun`. The amount is clicks times the price per click, but never more than the daily budget minus today's spend, and never below zero. Then it inserts an `AdBillingRun` row keyed by campaign and hour, with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. If the row already exists, nothing is returned and nothing is charged, so re-running the same hour is safe. If the insert worked and the amount is above zero, it posts an `AD_CHARGE` journal through `LedgerService`: the shop account is debited and the platform fees account is credited. The ledger post uses the same transaction, so the billing row and the journal either both exist or neither does. The daily job {{daily-reconciliation|reconciles}} later and reuses `charge` for hours that were missed.
out.summary: A cron job that bills each ad campaign for its valid clicks in the last full hour, once per hour, and never above the campaign's daily budget.

gotchas: The Redis INCRBY returns the value after increment; the code calculates the block start as `end - blockSize + 1` to claim the returned value and its 999 predecessors

The `pending` promise deduplicates concurrent lease() calls; if multiple nextId() requests arrive during a lease, they all wait for the same Redis round-trip
ID sequence gaps from crashed instances are expected and harmless; don't add logic to fill them
out.story: When you create a short link, you need a unique ID to scramble into a short code. Asking Redis for each ID would be slow. `IdLease` solves this with a ticket-server pattern: it leases a block of 1,000 IDs with one Redis call, hands them out from memory, and only fetches the next block when this one runs out. Every server instance does this independently without coordinating with the others. If a server crashes before using its entire batch, those IDs are skipped—which is harmless. The public API is just `nextId()`, which returns the next ID from the current batch, blocking only when a new batch needs to be leased from Redis. This lives in the marketing infra layer as part of {{share-short-links}}, feeding sequential IDs to the {{feistel-code-scrambler|Feistel scrambler}} that turns them into random-looking codes.
out.summary: IdLease leases a block of 1,000 sequential IDs from Redis with one call, then hands them out from memory to reduce database pressure.

If the Kafka transaction fails and aborts, the batch is re-read from the same starting offset, producing the same aggregates with the same tags. Downstream consumers use (campaign, minute, partition, first_offset) as the unique key for these aggregates, so a re-delivered aggregate replaces the prior one instead of creating a duplicate. This is how {{exactly-once-transaction|exactly-once delivery}} is achieved.

The SET succeeds only if the key doesn't already exist; success means this impression is being clicked for the first time in the 1-hour window, while failure means it's a repeat click. On repeat clicks, the handler returns immediately with the click marked `valid: false`. Duplicate impressions never reach [IP burst filtering]({{ip-burst-filter}}) or Kafka publishing. The user still gets redirected to the product page, preserving the browsing experience, but the click doesn't count toward billing or spend tracking.

out.story: When an ad click arrives, we check whether the IP address has already clicked too many times in the current minute. To avoid storing raw IPs in Redis, each IP is hashed with SHA-256 using the secret key as a salt. We maintain a Redis counter for each hashed IP per minute—the counter increments with each click and automatically expires to keep Redis clean. If the count exceeds 20, we mark the click as invalid (`valid: 0`) so it won't be charged to the advertiser, but we still record it to Kafka for auditing. This stops rapid-fire fraud from a single IP without unfairly blocking legitimate users who happen to click multiple times.

If the request header `x-edge-click-recorded` is not `1` (meaning the edge worker has not already counted it), it calls `recordClick`. That builds a `link.clicked` event with a fresh `uuidv7` click id, the code, a timestamp, the country (from the `cf-ipcountry` header), the referer cut to 300 characters, and a flag for whether it came via the edge. It sends the event to Kafka (topic `links.events`, keyed by code) without waiting, so the redirect is never slowed down, and a failed send is silently dropped. The redirect then adds `ref=<code>` to the destination so checkout can attribute the sale. For how links are created and resolved, see {{share-short-links}}. On the other side, `LinkClicksProjector` (name `link-clicks`) listens to the links topic. It keeps only events that match `LinkClicked`, reshapes each one into a row (`click_id`, `code`, `ts` without the trailing `Z`, `country`, `referer`, `via_edge` as 0 or 1) and bulk-inserts into the ClickHouse `link_clicks` table through `ClickHouseSink`. Duplicates are not removed on insert. The code comment says they are deduped by click id at merge time. The owner reads the numbers with `GET /links/:code/stats`. `stats` checks the link exists and belongs to the caller (otherwise 404), then queries `link_clicks_minute` for the last 7 days, summing clicks per minute.

out.story: Billing jobs can run twice for the same hour. The hourly job may be re-run with an explicit `hour`, and the daily reconcile can also call `charge` for an hour the hourly path missed. So `charge` in `AdBillingJobs` needs a hard guarantee that one campaign-hour never produces two charges. The guarantee is the `AdBillingRun` table. Its primary key is the campaign id plus the hour. `charge` opens a transaction, locks the campaign row with `FOR UPDATE`, and works out the amount. Then it runs `INSERT INTO "AdBillingRun" ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING "journalId"`. If the pair already exists, nothing comes back, and `charge` returns 0 without touching the ledger. If the insert did go through, `charge` posts the `AD_CHARGE` journal to the ledger in the same transaction, using the same `journalId`. Both writes commit together or roll back together. So there is never a billing row without a journal, or a journal without a billing row. The insert also happens when the amount is 0, so a capped-out hour is still marked as handled. See {{daily-budget-cap}} for how the amount is limited.
out.summary: Each campaign-and-hour pair is billed only once because `charge` inserts an `AdBillingRun` row, keyed by campaign and hour, in the same database transaction as the ledger journal.

gotchas: The 120-second expiry is twice the bucket width, not equal to it. This allows clicks arriving just after a minute boundary to still count in the old bucket.
The increment and expiry are sent together in a Redis pipeline (multi/exec) to ensure atomicity; if separate, a race condition could leave a counter without its TTL.
The minute number is not calendar-aligned (not 0–59); bucket 1234 is a 60-second window starting at timestamp 1234 * 60,000 ms.
Redis expiry is not guaranteed to be exact; a key might persist slightly past 120 seconds if the server is busy. Design defensively if exact timing matters.

parts.what: Dividing the current timestamp in milliseconds by 60,000 and flooring gives an integer that increments once per minute, providing a stable bucket ID for grouping clicks.

parts.what: The key `adclick:ip:${ipHash}:${minute}` stores an integer that increments with each click, used to track and limit how many times an IP can click in one minute.

parts.what: Each counter is set to expire 120 seconds after creation, cleaning up old buckets from Redis without manual deletion and providing a grace period for late-arriving clicks.

out.story: When a click arrives at the rate limiter, it needs to be counted against the per-IP limit that resets every minute. The {{minute-bucket-formula|time bucketing formula}} divides the current timestamp by 60,000 and floors it, producing a stable number that increments once per minute. Each IP gets its own {{redis-counter-per-ip-minute|counter}} under a key like `adclick:ip:${ipHash}:${minute}`. When a click arrives, the counter increments. If the count exceeds 20, the click is marked invalid but still recorded. To avoid accumulating stale buckets, each counter key {{120-second-expiry-ttl|expires automatically after 120 seconds}}—double the bucket width. This grace period allows clicks arriving just after a minute boundary to still count in the previous minute, and it cleans up Redis without explicit deletion logic.

out.story: When someone opens `GET /l/:code`, the service calls `resolve` in `ShareLinkService`. It first checks the code looks right: 4 to 32 letters, digits or dashes. Anything else gets `null` right away, with no lookups. Next it asks the Bloom filter (`RedisBloomFilter`, a compact Redis set that can say "definitely not a code" or "maybe") about the code. If the answer is "definitely not", `resolve` returns `null` and stops. That way, people scanning random codes never reach the cache or the database. If Redis fails, the check is treated as "maybe", so real links still work. Codes are added to the filter in `create` after they are saved. For "maybe" codes, `resolve` calls the cache helper `getOrLoad`, which loads the link from the `Links` DynamoDB table on a miss. Misses are cached for a short time too, so a repeated bad code doesn't hit DynamoDB each time. At the end, a link whose expiry time has passed is dropped and `null` is returned. The caller turns `null` into a 404. See {{share-short-links}} for the full create and redirect flow.

out.story: Everything lives in the `marketing` domain, wired by `ShareLinksModule`. `ShareLinksController` has four routes: `POST /links` creates a link, `GET /links` lists your own, `GET /links/:code/stats` shows click stats (see {{link-click-analytics}}), and `GET /l/:code` is the public redirect. The first three need a logged-in user. The redirect allows anonymous callers. When you create a link, `ShareLinkService.create` first checks the destination. Only `http(s)` URLs on the marketplace front-end host (or its `www.` twin) pass, so the shortener can't be used as an open redirect. It also strips any `ref` parameter from the URL. Then it makes the code. If you gave no alias, it takes the next number from {{id-lease}}, scrambles it with {{feistel-code-scrambler}}, and writes it in base62. If you gave an alias, it uses that. The link is saved in DynamoDB with a rule that the code must not exist yet, so a taken alias returns 409. The code is then added to a Bloom filter and any cached "not found" for it is dropped. When someone opens `/l/:code`, `resolve` checks the code format, then the Bloom filter (a quick way to say "this code was never created", which gives 404 with no lookup). Two Nest modules wire it up: `AdsModule` for the API side (controller, service, Kafka producer) and `AdsWorkerModule` for the worker side (click aggregation and billing jobs, using ClickHouse and the ledger). First, a seller creates a campaign with `POST /shops/:shopId/ads/campaigns`. It needs the `products.write` permission on that shop. Token checks, dedupe, fraud limits and Kafka publishing are covered in {{ad-click-tracking-and-fraud}}. For valid clicks, the campaign's price per click is added to its daily Redis spend counter, which is what `sponsored` reads next time. Billing from the clicks happens later, see {{ad-click-aggregation-and-billing}}.

gotchas: Transaction abort on error means failed batches are re-delivered automatically—not a manual retry in application code; the consumer will poll the same batch again from the old offset
The idempotent keying is safe only because aggregates are keyed with source_partition and first_offset; otherwise re-writing the same batch would double-count clicks
Consumer must use `readUncommitted: false` and `autoCommit: false` or the transaction pattern breaks—committed aggregates and offsets must stay perfectly in sync
Transactional producer needs a unique `transactionalId` per instance (built from hostname + pid) or fencing errors occur in multi-node setups
out.story: When a batch of clicks arrives from {{ad-click-tracking-and-fraud}}, the `ClickAggregator` consumes them from the `ads.clicks` topic. It groups the clicks by campaign and minute with `aggregateBatch`, counting valid and invalid clicks in each bucket. Then it opens a Kafka transaction. Within that transaction, it sends all the minute aggregates (each keyed by campaign id) to the `ads.click-aggregates` topic, and tells Kafka to commit the consumer group's offset for the batch—the position where the next batch will start. If all of this succeeds, the transaction commits. If anything fails mid-way (a network error, a producer timeout), the entire transaction aborts: no aggregates are visible, and the offsets stay unchanged, so the batch is automatically re-delivered on the next poll. This atomic pattern ensures exactly-once delivery: every click in the batch is counted in exactly one aggregate, never skipped and never duplicated, even if the service crashes in the middle.
out.summary: Sends minute aggregates and commits consumer offsets in one Kafka transaction, ensuring both succeed together or both fail and re-deliver the batch.

out.story: A click token pairs a base64url-encoded claims object with a truncated HMAC-SHA256 signature in the format `payload.mac`, created by {{sign-click}}. `verifyClick` recomputes the HMAC signature from the payload, verifies it matches the received signature in constant time, decodes the claims from base64url JSON, and checks that the expiry time `e` is in the future. Any validation failure returns `null`. In {{ad-click-tracking-and-fraud}}, `verifyClick` ensures that a click token is legitimate and not stale. Ads can only be charged for impressions within 30 minutes of being shown, so expired or forged tokens are rejected before the click is tracked or billed.

parts.what: A two-step Lua script that first tries to set a 14-day marker for the journal, and if successful, atomically increments each account's balance in the Redis hash in a single loop.

out.story: Each time {{recording-money-in-ledger|money is recorded in the ledger}}, a `JournalPosted` event flows to the `BalanceProjector`. The projector extracts the journal's lines (account ID and signed amount pairs) and calls the `APPLY_JOURNAL` Lua script atomically in Redis. The script first attempts to set a per-journal idempotency marker with a 14-day expiry. If the marker already exists (duplicate journal redelivered), the script returns 0 and skips the update. If the marker is new, the script atomically increments each account's balance in the `ledger:balances` Redis hash and returns 1. This design eliminates the "hot account" bottleneck: the platform fee account is updated in every sale. Database row locks would serialize access, but Redis Lua atomic execution keeps throughput high and latency low.

out.story: When a journal is posted to the ledger (via {{recording-money-in-ledger}}), it emits a `JournalPosted` event. The `BalanceProjector` catches that event and applies its lines to a Redis hash of account balances. But events redeliver from Kafka, so the projector uses a single Lua script to guarantee atomic, idempotent updates. The script first tries to set a unique marker key for this journal (with a 14-day TTL). If the marker already exists, the script stops and returns 0—the journal was already applied, so skip it. If it's new, the script increments each account's balance in the Redis hash by that line's amount, then returns 1. This design solves a classic problem: if you stored each account's balance in a database row, every sale would contend on the hot accounts (like the platform fee account that every transaction touches). Here, since `HINCRBY` on a hash field is atomic, multiple concurrent journals never row-lock—Redis handles concurrency internally.

If the hash has no entry, or Redis fails, `balance` returns `{ available: await ledger.balance(account), source: 'ledger' }`. This is the authoritative SQL sum from `LedgerService`.

parts.title: Idempotent creation of the payment row
parts.what: An insert with `ON CONFLICT ("idempotencyKey") DO NOTHING`, so a duplicate or retried message finds the existing payment rather than creating a second one.

parts.title: Marking a timed-out Stripe charge as UNKNOWN
parts.what: If Stripe's outcome is unknown, the payment becomes `UNKNOWN` and the retry reuses the same Stripe idempotency key, so the original result comes back instead of a second charge.

parts.what: A cheap pre-check, then an `UPDATE "Product"` that only succeeds when `quantity >= :quantity` and bumps `version`. This is the real guard against overselling.

parts.title: Refund when stock runs out after charging
parts.what: When the stock update finds no row, the service refunds the Stripe payment intent outside the transaction, then marks the payment `REFUNDED` and notifies the caller.

out.story: Payment requests arrive on the `payments.requests` Kafka topic. `handlePayment` in `PaymentController` hands each message to the shared Kafka consumer helper. That helper knows the response topic (`PAYMENTS_RESPONSES`) and the dead-letter topic (`PAYMENTS_DLQ`). The real work happens in `PaymentService.executePayment`. First, `executePayment` makes sure a `Payment` row exists for the request's idempotency key (a unique key that marks duplicate requests as the same request). It uses `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, then reads the row back. If the payment is already `COMPLETED`, `FAILED` or `REFUNDED`, it returns it at once. `PENDING` and `UNKNOWN` payments keep going. If a product is involved, a cheap stock check runs next. When stock is too low, it reports `Domain_InsufficientStockError` and stops before touching Stripe. Then it calls Stripe's `createPaymentIntent` with the same idempotency key, with no DB transaction held open. If Stripe times out, the payment is marked `UNKNOWN`, because the card may have been charged. The error is rethrown so Kafka retries it. Afterwards, one "Finalize Transaction" DB transaction does the rest. On success it decrements stock with a version-checked `UPDATE`. It then sets the payment to `COMPLETED`, books the sale with {{recording-money-in-ledger|the ledger}}, and writes the result to the outbox. On a Stripe failure it sets `FAILED` and writes a `Domain_StripePaymentFailed` outbox message. If the stock update matches no rows, someone else bought the last item. In that case the service refunds the Stripe charge, marks the payment `REFUNDED`, and reports the stock error through the outbox. A later job, described in {{resolving-unknown-payments}}, also settles `UNKNOWN` payments.
out.summary: A Kafka consumer that takes a payment request, charges the card through Stripe exactly once, records the result, and refunds the buyer if the product sold out in the meantime.

parts.title: Fixed namespace UUID used for every payout follow-up journal id
parts.what: `PAYOUT_NS` is a hard-coded UUID that scopes the UUIDv5 hashing, so these ids are stable and never collide with ids derived elsewhere.

parts.title: Function that builds the follow-up journal id from payout id and step
parts.what: `deriveJournalId` hashes `payoutId:step` with UUIDv5 under `PAYOUT_NS`, where the step is `sent` or `reversal`.

out.story: A payout first posts its own journal using the payout id itself as the journal id (done in `run`, the `payouts.run-weekly` handler). After that, the `payouts.send` handler in `PayoutJobs` has to post a second journal: either money sent, or a reversal. That second journal cannot reuse the payout id, because it is already taken. So `deriveJournalId` builds a new id from the payout id plus the step name. It joins the two as `payoutId:step` and hashes that text with UUIDv5 inside a fixed namespace constant, `PAYOUT_NS`. UUIDv5 is a pure hash: same input, same output. The `sent` and `reversal` steps give two different ids for the same payout, and the same step always gives the same id. In `send`, a successful Stripe transfer posts the `sent` journal (`PAYOUT_CLEARING` → `PAYOUTS_SENT`). A definite failure posts the `reversal` journal (`PAYOUT_CLEARING` → the shop's account). If the job runs again, it computes the same id, so the ledger can recognise the journal as a duplicate instead of counting it twice. See {{ledger-posting-model}} for the full money flow and {{send-failure-handling}} for when each branch runs.
out.summary: `deriveJournalId` turns a payout id and a step name (`sent` or `reversal`) into a fixed UUIDv5, so the follow-up ledger journal for a payout always gets the same id and a retry cannot post it twice.

parts.title: PostgreSQL advisory lock to serialize concurrent attempts
parts.what: `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(journalId))` acquires a transaction-scoped lock on the journalId hash, blocking concurrent transactions from processing the same settlement simultaneously.

parts.title: Existence check to detect already-posted settlements
parts.what: A `SELECT EXISTS` query inside the transaction checks if `LedgerEntry` already contains an entry with the journalId; if it does, the settlement is skipped because it was already posted.

out.story: This is the mechanism that ensures a settlement journal posts exactly once, even if Kafka redelivers the same `order.paid` event multiple times. It lives in the `SettlementListener`, which reacts to each order payment and must record how the net amount (total minus platform fee) is split among the shops in that order. To make settlement idempotent, the listener generates a deterministic `journalId` using UUIDv5 of the order ID and a fixed namespace—the same order ID always produces the same journalId, even on retries. Then it runs a database transaction that acquires a PostgreSQL advisory lock on the journalId hash (serializing concurrent attempts), checks if any `LedgerEntry` with that journalId already exists (if so, skips), and otherwise calls {{recording-money-in-ledger}} to post the journal. The combination of advisory lock and existence check in the same transaction guarantees exactly-once semantics: the first attempt posts the journalId; any concurrent or retried attempt finds it locked or finds the existing entry and skips.
out.summary: A deterministic UUIDv5 journalId, PostgreSQL advisory lock, and transaction-scoped existence check ensure settlement journals post exactly once despite Kafka redeliveries.

out.story: This step lives inside the `Finalize Transaction` block of `PaymentService.executePayment`. It runs only when Stripe says the charge `succeeded` and the request has a `productId`. Before charging, the service did a cheap stock look-up. That look-up can be wrong if another buyer grabs the stock in between, so this update is the real guard. See {{optimistic-stock-deduction}} for the full idea. The {{guarded-stock-update-query}} subtracts the quantity, adds 1 to `version`, and matches the row only when `quantity >= :quantity`. It runs in the same database transaction as the payment status update. The code then reads {{row-count-check}}: the number of rows the update changed. If the row count is 0, stock ran out after the card was charged. The code returns early with a {{needs-refund-result}}. The payment stays `PENDING`, and no ledger entry or success message is written. The caller then refunds Stripe outside the transaction and marks the payment `REFUNDED`. See {{refund-saga}}. If the row count is 1, the code carries on to mark the payment `COMPLETED` and post the ledger journal.
out.summary: After Stripe has charged the card, one guarded SQL `UPDATE` takes the bought quantity out of the product's stock, and only if enough stock is still there.

parts.title: The three types of reconciliation mismatches
parts.what: `MISSING_IN_LEDGER` means Stripe charged but we have no matching Payment record; `MISSING_AT_PROVIDER` means we have a record but Stripe never charged that key; `AMOUNT_MISMATCH` means both exist but the amounts differ.

parts.title: ReconciliationRun: the idempotence mechanism
parts.what: One row per (provider, day) pair; upserted at the start of each run. If `finishedAt` is already set, the job exits; if null, the job processes the day and sets `finishedAt` when done.

out.story: Every night at 02:30 UTC, the `payments.reconcile-daily` job streams Stripe payment charges from the past day and compares them with our payment records, matching each one by idempotency key. Stripe stores the key in the payment intent's metadata as `idempotencyKey`; we store it in our `Payment` record. The job loads all our COMPLETED payments for that day indexed by their key, then streams Stripe charges one at a time (using constant memory). For each charge that succeeded and has a matching key, it looks up our Payment record and compares the amounts. Any mismatch gets recorded in the `ReconciliationIssue` table: either a Stripe charge we don't have a record for (`MISSING_IN_LEDGER`), a payment we recorded that Stripe doesn't know about (`MISSING_AT_PROVIDER`), or an amount difference (`AMOUNT_MISMATCH`). The job is idempotent per (provider, day). It upserts into `ReconciliationRun` at the start: if a run for that day already finished, the job exits immediately; if it crashed and reruns, the old issues are deleted and recalculated from scratch. This prevents duplicate issue records on retries and makes the job safe to reschedule.
out.summary: Every night, the reconciliation job streams Stripe charges and matches them against our Payment records by idempotency key, recording any mismatches for investigation.

parts.title: Insert that silently skips when the idempotency key already exists
parts.what: A raw SQL `INSERT INTO "Payment"` with a generated id and `PENDING` status, ending in `ON CONFLICT ("idempotencyKey") DO NOTHING`.

parts.title: Read-back of the payment row in the same transaction
parts.what: After the insert, `requestPayment` loads the row by idempotency key together with its order, so new and duplicate messages get the same payment.

parts.title: Early return for payments already finished
parts.what: If the loaded payment is neither `PENDING` nor `UNKNOWN`, `executePayment` returns it without charging again.

out.story: The first thing `executePayment` (in `PaymentService`) does is open a short database transaction and try to insert a new `Payment` row. The row starts in `PENDING` status and carries the idempotency key, the amount, the order id and the user id. The idempotency key is the request ID that identifies this one purchase attempt. If a row with that key already exists, the insert does nothing and raises no error. This happens when the user spams the API or when Kafka redelivers the message. Right after the insert, in the same transaction, the code reads the payment back by idempotency key through `PaymentDtoService.requestPayment`. The first message and any duplicate both get the same row. If the server dies before the transaction commits, it rolls back. The Kafka offset does not move, so the message is retried and the row is created again. If the server dies just after the commit, the row stays `PENDING` and the next attempt picks it up. If the row is already `COMPLETED` or `FAILED`, `executePayment` returns it right away. `PENDING` and `UNKNOWN` rows carry on to the Stripe charge.
out.summary: A single SQL insert at the start of `executePayment` that creates the `Payment` row with `ON CONFLICT ("idempotencyKey") DO NOTHING`, then reads the row back, so retried or duplicate messages share one payment.

uses.how: Relies on the `Payment` model, its `PENDING` status and `PaymentDtoService.requestPayment` to read the row back.
This is the first step of the charging flow, which continues to stock checks and Stripe after the row exists.

gotchas: The insert is a raw SQL query, not a Sequelize `create`, so model defaults do not apply. The id, `createdAt` and `updatedAt` are set in the SQL itself.
`DO NOTHING` returns no error and does not say whether a row was inserted. The code always reads the row back to learn what exists.
A duplicate message does not insert, but it gets the existing payment back. If that payment is `UNKNOWN`, it continues and re-sends to Stripe with the same key.
Only the `idempotencyKey` conflict is ignored. A different failure, such as a bad `bisOrderId`, still raises an error.
out.story: At the start of `executePayment`, inside a database transaction, the service runs a raw `INSERT INTO "Payment"`. The row gets a database-generated id (`gen_random_uuid()`), the idempotency key from the request, the amount, the user and order ids, and status `PENDING`. The statement ends with `ON CONFLICT ("idempotencyKey") DO NOTHING`. If no payment has that key yet, the row is created. If one already exists (a Kafka redelivery, a retry after a crash, or a user spamming the API), the insert quietly does nothing and raises no error. Either way, the same transaction then reads the payment back by idempotency key with `requestPayment`, so every caller ends up holding the one shared row. The status of that row decides what happens next. See {{idempotent-payment-insert}} for the wider flow. A payment that is no longer `PENDING` or `UNKNOWN` is returned straight away. Otherwise the charge goes on. The insert relies on a unique constraint on `idempotencyKey`, which is what `ON CONFLICT` targets.
out.summary: A raw SQL insert at the start of `executePayment` that creates the `Payment` row as `PENDING` and silently does nothing if a row with the same idempotency key already exists.

gotchas: All amounts are integers in cents; no floating-point math, so rounding must be solved algorithmically.
Shops are sorted before allocation to ensure deterministic output—the same inputs always produce the same share order.

out.story: When an order with multiple shops is paid, the net amount (total minus platform fee) must be split across the shops that fulfilled it. Simply dividing proportionally can leave a few cents unaccounted for due to rounding. The largest-remainder allocation algorithm solves this: it calculates each shop's proportional share, then systematically gives any remaining cents to the shops with the largest fractional parts. The result is an array of amounts that sum exactly to the net amount—not a penny more or less. In {{settling-orders-to-shops}}, when an `order.paid` event arrives, the settlement listener groups line totals by shop, sorts shops alphabetically for determinism, and calls `allocate()` with the net amount and each shop's total. It gets back an array of allocated amounts, one per shop in sorted order. This array then becomes the credit side of a SETTLEMENT journal: each shop account is credited with its allocated share.
out.summary: A mathematical algorithm that distributes a net amount proportionally across shops based on their line totals, ensuring the sum equals the exact net amount to the cent with no rounding loss.

data.how: A BIGINT column storing the signed amount in cents for each journal line; the database enforces that all lines in a journal sum to zero.

gotchas: Stored in cents, not dollars—$1.00 is `100`, not `1`; raw DB values look deceptively small.
Immutable once posted—errors cannot be fixed by updating an amount; you must post a reversal entry.
Every journal must sum to zero—the database rejects any set of entries that don't balance, even if off by one cent.
out.story: Every line in the ledger (a {{ledger-entry-row}}) has an `amount`—a single number that is positive or negative. Positive means money came in (a credit); negative means money went out (a debit). Using a signed integer is mathematically cleaner than keeping separate `debit` and `credit` columns; you just add all the amounts up, and they must sum to zero. The amount is always in cents, never dollars. So $1.00 is stored as `100`, not `1`. This keeps all numbers as integers and dodges the floating-point rounding errors that break financial systems. Once an entry is written, its amount is immutable—you can never update it. If you make a mistake, you post a reversal entry instead. The {{recording-money-in-ledger}} process enforces that every journal balances: debits and credits are just the sign of the amount.
out.summary: The `amount` field stores money in cents as a signed integer: positive for credits (money in), negative for debits (money out).

out.story: A `LedgerEntry` is the smallest unit in the ledger: one line saying "account X gained or lost Y cents." When {{recording-money-in-ledger|LedgerService posts a journal}}, it creates one entry per account involved—buyer, seller, platform—all tagged with the same `journalId` so they stay together. The rows never change after creation (`updatedAt` and `deletedAt` are both disabled in the schema), so once the ledger says something happened, it stays true. The `amount` field uses positive for credits (money in) and negative for debits (money out). A `journalId` groups all the lines of a balanced posting together; the database rejects any journal whose lines don't sum to exactly zero, enforcing double-entry bookkeeping. Each entry also stores `kind` (like `SALE`, `SETTLEMENT`, `PAYOUT`) and an optional `paymentId` link back to the {{payment-records|Payment}} that triggered it.

steps.text: `recordMarketplaceSale` is called with `paymentId`, the buyer, merchant and platform revenue account ids, `totalAmount`, `feeAmount` and a `tx`. It wraps its work in `DbUtilsService.wrapInTransaction`, passing `tx`.
It rejects `totalAmount < feeAmount` with an `InternalServerErrorException`.
It computes `buyerDebit = -|totalAmount|`, `merchantCredit = |totalAmount - feeAmount|` and `platformCredit = |feeAmount|`. It throws if the three do not sum to 0.
It calls `post()` with `journalId = paymentId`, `kind: 'SALE'`, the `paymentId` and the three lines.
`post()` sums the line amounts. It throws an `InternalServerErrorException` ('CRITICAL: unbalanced journal') if the sum is not 0 or any amount fails `Number.isSafeInteger`.

`post()` drops zero-amount lines. It then calls `ledgerEntryModel.bulkCreate` with `validate: true` inside the caller's transaction. Each row carries `journalId`, `kind`, `paymentId ?? null`, `accountId` and `amount: BigInt(l.amount)`.

`post()` then calls `domainEvents.record(JournalPosted.create(journalId, 1, { kind, lines }), tx)`. The event is defined with `defineEvent('ledger.journal_posted', 'ledger', 1, ...)` and a zod schema for `kind` and `lines`. The outbox row commits or rolls back with the ledger rows.

`balance(accountId, tx?)` runs a raw `SELECT coalesce(sum(amount), 0)::bigint` on `"LedgerEntry"`. This is the authoritative balance. The Redis projection is the fast path, and `balance()` is the fallback and rebuild source.

out.story: The ledger stores financial transactions as immutable `LedgerEntry` rows in a double-entry bookkeeping system where every journal must sum to zero. Two scheduled jobs keep this system healthy and performant. The `ledger.ensure-partitions` job runs at 3 AM on the 1st of each month and pre-creates partitions for the months ahead by calling the `ledger_ensure_partitions()` SQL function. This prevents new inserts from accidentally landing in a default catch-all partition when they don't match any existing date range. By default it creates 4 months worth of partitions. The `ledger.verify-invariants` job runs daily at 2:15 AM and acts as a belt-and-braces check on top of the commit-time trigger: it queries the entire `LedgerEntry` table to confirm the book balance is zero, and also checks that no journal from the last 2 days is unbalanced (each journal's entries should sum to zero). If any violation is found—like entries inserted by a manual script with the trigger disabled—it increments a counter, logs an error, and pages someone on-call.

out.story: Every payout is a set of ledger journals tied to one `Payout` row. When the weekly job picks a shop, it posts a journal that takes the full balance out of the shop account and parks it in the holding account `PAYOUT_CLEARING`. The journal id is simply the payout id, and this happens in the same transaction that inserts the `Payout` row. Later the send job asks Stripe to move the money. If Stripe accepts, the money moves from `PAYOUT_CLEARING` to `PAYOUTS_SENT` (a platform account that totals what has left). If Stripe definitely refuses, the same amount moves from `PAYOUT_CLEARING` back to the shop account as a reversal. Either follow-up only posts if the payout row was still `PENDING` and the update changed it. Retries must never post the same journal twice. So the follow-up ids are made by {{derive-journal-id}}, which turns the payout id plus a step name into the same UUID every time. The week itself is chosen by {{monday-of}}, so a re-run in the same week hits the unique shop and week key. The posting itself is done by {{recording-money-in-ledger|the ledger service}}.

out.story: `mondayOf` is a small exported helper at the bottom of `payout.jobs.ts`. It answers one question: which Monday does this date's week start on? The answer is always in UTC, never in the server's local time zone. It works in three steps. First it rebuilds the date at midnight UTC, so the time of day is dropped. Then it steps back by the number of days since Monday (the `(getUTCDay() + 6) % 7` trick turns Sunday-first day numbers into Monday-first ones, so Monday is 0 and Sunday is 6). Last it formats the result with `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` to get `YYYY-MM-DD`. The weekly job `payouts.run-weekly` uses it when it runs. If the job payload has no `periodStart`, it calls `mondayOf(new Date())` to pick the current week. That string is saved as the payout's `periodStart`. Together with the shop, it forms the unique key that stops a second payout for the same shop and week. See {{weekly-seller-payouts}} and {{period-start-weekly-identifier}}.

out.story: Inside `PaymentService.executePayment`, stock is checked twice. First comes a plain `SELECT quantity FROM "Product"`. If the product is missing or has too little stock, the service sends a `Domain_InsufficientStockError` through the outbox and returns the payment. No Stripe call is made. This check is only a shortcut to avoid a pointless charge and refund. It does not stop two buyers racing. The real guard comes after Stripe says the charge `succeeded`. Inside the finalize transaction, one `UPDATE "Product"` subtracts the quantity, adds 1 to `version`, and only matches rows where `quantity >= :quantity`. The service reads the row count. If it is 0, someone else took the stock first. In that case the function returns early with `needsRefund: true`. The payment stays `PENDING`, and no ledger entry is written. After the transaction ends, the service refunds the charge. This follows {{refund-saga}}. If the update matched a row, the normal path continues: update the payment status, then record the sale in the ledger. See {{charging-a-payment}} for the whole flow.

gotchas: Exactly-once rests on three things together: the deterministic UUIDv5 `journalId`, the advisory lock and the `EXISTS` check, all inside one transaction. Dropping any one weakens the guarantee.
The shop ids are sorted before allocation, and `allocate` is deterministic. A redelivery therefore produces the same shares in the same order.
Orders with no `shopId` lines are silently skipped and produce no journal.
The net amount is clamped to 0 when the total is below `PLATFORM_FEE_MINOR`. A journal with zero shares can still be posted in that case.
Shop shares are weighted by line totals (`price * quantity`), not by the net amount. The platform fee is taken off the total first, so it is not split by shop.

steps.text: The `SettlementListener` projector is registered with name `order-settlement` and subscribes to `OrderPaid.topic`. The projection infrastructure calls `project(events)` with a batch of `EventEnvelope`s.

`project()` loops over the batch and runs `OrderPaid.match(raw)` on each envelope. Envelopes that don't match are skipped. Matching ones go to `settle(event.aggregateId, event.payload)`, where the aggregate id is the order id.
`settle()` keeps only the lines that have a `shopId`. If none do, it returns without writing anything.
It sums `price * quantity` per shop into a `Map`, then sorts the shop ids so the order is deterministic.

It computes `net = max(0, paid.total - PLATFORM_FEE_MINOR)`. It then calls `allocate(net, shopTotals)` to get each shop's share by largest-remainder allocation. The shares add back up to `net` exactly.
It derives `journalId = uuidv5('settlement:<orderId>', SETTLEMENT_NS)`. The same order therefore always gets the same journal id.
It opens a Sequelize transaction and takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(journalId))`. This serialises concurrent handling of the same order.
Inside the same transaction it runs `SELECT EXISTS` on `"LedgerEntry"` for that `journalId`. If a row exists, the settlement was already posted and it returns.

Otherwise it calls `ledger.post()` with `kind: 'SETTLEMENT'` and passes the transaction. The lines are a `-net` entry on `LEDGER_ACCOUNTS.CLEARING` plus one `shopAccount(shopId)` entry per shop with its share. `paymentId` is `null` when the id starts with `pay_`.

out.summary: `SettlementListener` is an `order-settlement` projector that consumes `order.paid` events. For each paid order it splits the net amount (order total minus `PLATFORM_FEE_MINOR`) across the shops in the order by largest-remainder allocation. It then posts one `SETTLEMENT` journal through `LedgerService.post()`. That journal debits `CLEARING` and credits each `SHOP_<id>` account, which records what the platform owes each shop. Redelivery is safe because the journal id is deterministic and guarded by a lock and an existence check.

steps.text: `PaymentDtoModule` registers `Payment` via `SequelizeModule.forFeature([Payment])`, provides and exports `PaymentDtoService`, and imports `ApiConfigModule` and `AuthModule`. It has no controllers.

The `Payment` model defines columns `id` (UUID, default `uuidv7()`), `idempotencyKey`, `amount` (BIGINT), `status` (ENUM of `PaymentStatus`), `userId`, `bisOrderId` (foreign key to the orders `BisOrderModel`) and nullable `providerRef` (Stripe PaymentIntent id once known). It has `BelongsTo` `bisOrder`, `HasMany` `ledgerEntries` (`LedgerEntry`, foreign key `paymentId`), and the index `idx_payment_user_id_desc` on `u…

`PaymentStatus` has the values `PENDING`, `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELLED`, `REFUNDED` and `UNKNOWN`. `UNKNOWN` means the provider call timed out, so the charge may or may not exist. It is resolved by asking the provider (SD-20).

The `PaymentScope.WithAll` scope takes `PaymentWithAllFilters`. It builds a `where` from `id`, `idempotencyKey`, `status` and `amount`, but only for values that are truthy. It applies `attributes` as given. If `bisOrderFilters` is set, it includes `bisOrder` using `BisOrderModel.scope` with `BisOrderScope.WithAll`. That include is `required` only when `bisOrderRequired` is true.
`PaymentDtoService.countAll`, `findAll` and `findOne` apply `Payment.scope({ method: [PaymentScope.WithAll, params] })` and run `count`, `findAll` or `findOne` with the optional transaction `tx`.

`requestPayment` validates the optional `additors`; only type `'stub'` is accepted, and any other type throws `BadRequestException`. It then calls `findOne` and throws `Fatal_NotFoundError` ('Payment not found') if nothing matches. `requestPayments` does the same validation and returns `findAll`.
`requestPaymentOptional` wraps `requestPayment`. It returns `null` when `Fatal_NotFoundError` is thrown and rethrows all other errors.

`create` calls `paymentModel.create(params, { transaction: tx })`. `update` calls `paymentModel.update` with `where`, `returning: true` and the transaction. It returns the first updated row and throws `Fatal_NotFoundError` ('Payment is not updated') if zero rows were affected or no row came back.

out.story: Every week, a job creates one `Payout` row for each shop that has enough balance and moves the money in the ledger (see {{recording-money-in-ledger}}). A second job sends each pending payout through Stripe Connect and records the Stripe reference. If Stripe refuses, the payout is marked `FAILED`, the failure reason is stored, and the ledger journal is reversed. The model lives in the `Payout` table. The key to idempotency is a database-level `UNIQUE(shopId, periodStart)` constraint: if a job runs twice in the same week (a retry or crash recovery), the duplicate insert fails gracefully. Together with the ledger's idempotency, this ensures each weekly run is exactly once.

out.story: Every payout is for one shop in one week, and that week is identified by its Monday date. When the weekly payout job runs, it calculates the start of the current or target week (using the {{monday-of}} helper), and uses that as `periodStart`. out.story: Double-entry bookkeeping requires every journal to balance: debits equal credits. out.story: Money moves in the ledger as a *journal*: a group of lines, each line being an account and a signed whole-number amount in cents. Positive means money in (credit), negative means money out (debit). A journal must add up to exactly zero. `LedgerService` lives in `libs/domains/payments/application/ledger.service.ts` and is exported by `LedgerModule`. Everything goes through `LedgerService.post()`. It first checks that the lines sum to zero and that every amount is a safe integer. If not, it throws a 500 `CRITICAL: unbalanced journal`. Then it writes one `LedgerEntry` row per non-zero line with `bulkCreate`, inside the transaction the caller passes in. Last, it records a `JournalPosted` event (`ledger.journal_posted`) through the outbox in that same transaction. So the rows and the event commit together or not at all. The code comments say a deferred `ledger_balanced` constraint trigger in the database re-checks the sum at COMMIT as a last line of defense. That trigger is not in the files shown here. `recordMarketplaceSale()` is the sale helper. It splits a payment into three lines: the buyer is debited the full total, the merchant is credited total minus fee, and the platform revenue account is credited the fee. It uses the payment id as the journal id, so there is one `SALE` journal per payment. `balance()` gives the authoritative balance of an account by summing its entries. It is the fallback for the fast Redis balance, see {{shop-balance-read-model}}.

Then it opens the finalize transaction and runs the {{optimistic-stock-deduction}} update. If that update changes zero rows, someone else bought the last items while we were charging. The service does not touch the `Payment` row. It leaves it `PENDING` and returns a result with `needsRefund: true` and the Stripe payment intent id. out.story: Payments get stuck in `UNKNOWN` status when Stripe queries time out and Kafka retries exhaust. Every 5 minutes, the `payments.resolve-unknown` job wakes up and finds all payments with status `UNKNOWN` that haven't been updated for at least 5 minutes. This delay gives Kafka retries time to finish before we start asking Stripe; without it, we'd be querying too early and wasting effort. The job limits to 100 payments per run to avoid overload. For each stuck payment, it calls `StripeService.findPaymentIntentByIdempotencyKey()` using the payment's idempotency key—the request ID we sent with the original charge. Stripe stores this key on the intent, so we can find the payment even though we never got the response. Once we know the real outcome, the job settles the payment atomically: it updates the payment status, records a marketplace sale journal if the charge succeeded (via {{recording-money-in-ledger}}), and publishes the result to `payments.responses` Kafka topic through the outbox. If Stripe has never seen the idempotency key and 60 minutes have passed since the payment was created, the job gives up and marks it `FAILED`, so stuck payments don't linger forever.

The `payments.resolve-unknown` job wakes up every 5 minutes and hunts for payments that have been stuck for at least 5 minutes. For each one, it asks Stripe "did you charge this idempotency key?" without ever creating a new charge. Stripe usually has an answer: if the intent succeeded, the job settles the payment as `COMPLETED` and records the money in the ledger just like a normal success. If Stripe says it was canceled or needs a payment method, the job settles as `FAILED`. If Stripe never saw it and 60 minutes have passed, the job gives up and settles as `FAILED` (it probably never reached the network). In all cases, settlement posts a journal through {{recording-money-in-ledger}} and publishes a payment response to Kafka so orders, notifications, and the shop balance read-model all react exactly as they would to a normal result. The whole settlement is one database transaction: the payment status updates, the ledger journal posts, and the outbox notification queues together. parts.what: Updates `status` and `providerRef` only when the WHERE clause finds `status = UNKNOWN` still true, so a concurrent settlement attempt finds zero rows and exits without duplicate work.

out.story: Part of {{resolving-unknown-payments}}, this job runs every 5 minutes to rescue payments that timed out when charging. It finds all payments in UNKNOWN status that have been stuck for at least 5 minutes. For each one, it queries Stripe by idempotency key to learn whether the charge actually succeeded. If Stripe says yes, the payment is settled as COMPLETED. If Stripe shows it was canceled or failed, or if 60 minutes have passed and Stripe never saw the request, it's settled as FAILED. When a payment completes, the job records a {{record-marketplace-sale|marketplace sale journal}} in the ledger—debiting the buyer, crediting the merchant minus their fee, and crediting the platform for the fee amount. For all outcomes (completed or failed), it publishes the settlement result to Kafka so orders, clients, and the balance projection stay in sync. The payment status update, ledger post, and outbox notification all happen in a single transaction: if any step fails, they all roll back together. The WHERE clause that checks `status = UNKNOWN` before updating is the guard against duplicates. If this job runs twice on the same payment (or Kafka retries settle it), the second attempt finds the status no longer UNKNOWN and exits silently—already done, no work needed.
out.summary: Atomically settles payments stuck in UNKNOWN status by querying Stripe, recording marketplace sales to the ledger, and publishing responses through the outbox.

data.name: PostgreSQL advisory lock

gotchas: Advisory locks are database-level, not process-level. If you run multiple app instances, they coordinate through the database. Plan for potential lock contention if many orders settle simultaneously.
The lock is transaction-scoped. If your transaction takes too long, it blocks other settlements. Keep the settlement logic fast—do not call slow external services while holding the lock.
`hashtext()` is necessary because PostgreSQL advisory locks accept a `bigint`, not text. The call would fail with a type error if you passed the journalId string directly.

The lock alone is not sufficient for idempotency. If you remove the existence check, duplicate settlements can still occur due to race conditions between lock release and journal insert. You need both parts.

parts.title: Advisory lock acquisition on journalId hash
parts.what: The `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(journalId))` call that acquires an exclusive lock on the hashed journalId, blocking concurrent attempts to settle the same order.

parts.title: Existence check: verify settlement not already posted
parts.what: The `SELECT EXISTS` query that confirms the settlement was not already posted to the ledger in a prior attempt, providing the second half of the idempotency guarantee.

out.story: When a settlement event arrives from Kafka, multiple instances of your service might receive and process the same `order.paid` message. Without coordination, they'd all try to post the settlement journal to the ledger independently, creating duplicates. {{settling-orders-to-shops|SettlementListener}} prevents this by acquiring an advisory lock on a hashed version of the journalId before checking and posting. The lock works in three steps. First, a deterministic journalId is generated using UUIDv5 of the order—the same order always produces the same ID. Then, inside a database transaction, `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(journalId))` acquires an exclusive lock on that ID's hash, blocking any other transaction trying to lock the same journalId. Finally, an existence check queries whether the settlement was already posted to `LedgerEntry`; if it exists, the method returns early and the duplicate is discarded. The lock is held only for the duration of the transaction, so it does not starve other work. PostgreSQL's advisory locks work at the database level, not the process level, so even if you run multiple instances of the service, they coordinate through the database. Together with the deterministic ID and the existence check, the advisory lock implements the {{exactly-once-settlement}} pattern for settlements.
out.summary: A PostgreSQL transaction-scoped advisory lock acquired on a deterministic settlement identifier that serializes concurrent transactions processing the same order, preventing duplicate settlement journals despite Kafka message redelivery.

parts.title: Exactly-once guarantee with UUIDv5, advisory lock, and existence check
parts.what: A deterministic journalId (UUIDv5 of the order), a PostgreSQL advisory lock, and a transaction-scoped existence check in the ledger prevent duplicate settlements from redelivered Kafka events.

out.story: Every time an order is marked paid, an `order.paid` event arrives. The settlement listener reads it and extracts all the line items that belong to shops (filtering out platform items). It groups these lines by shopId and sums the price of each shop's items to figure out what share of the order came from each shop. The listener then calculates the net settlement amount: the order total minus the platform fee. This net is divided across the shops proportionally to their share using a largest-remainder allocation—a deterministic algorithm that ensures the amounts sum to the exact cent with no rounding loss. The settlement records a double-entry journal: it debits (clears money from) the CLEARING account and credits each shop's account with their share—what we owe them. Because Kafka may redeliver the same event, the listener guarantees exactly-once settlement using three techniques in a single database transaction: a deterministic journalId computed as a UUIDv5 of the order ID, a PostgreSQL advisory lock, and an existence check in the ledger. If the settlement has already posted, the check detects it and skips the duplicate. The journal posts through {{concept:domain/payments/recording-money-in-ledger|LedgerService}}, which emits a `JournalPosted` event that drives balance reads and payout calculations downstream.
out.summary: When an order is paid, the `SettlementListener` splits the net amount (total minus platform fee) across the shops in the order and records each shop's share as a credit in the ledger—their balance that they can later claim as a payout.

out.story: When money moves through the ledger (see {{recording-money-in-ledger}}), a `JournalPosted` event is emitted. The `BalanceProjector` catches these events and applies them to account balances stored in Redis. This denormalized view is fast—a balance read is a single Redis HGET, not a million-row sum—and stays consistent: a Lua script ensures each journal is applied at most once, even if the event is redelivered. When a shop hits `GET /shops/:shopId/balance`, the API reads from the Redis cache; if the projection hasn't caught up yet, it falls back to the authoritative ledger query. The same endpoint also serves payout history: `GET /shops/:shopId/payouts` returns the 52 most recent weekly payouts (created by {{weekly-seller-payouts}}), ordered by period start date.
